quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The architect who designed the new library, which opened last spring, also designed our city hall. What is the antecedent of 'which opened last spring'?
quests.completedSentence: The architect who designed the new library, which opened last spring, also designed our city hall. What is the antecedent of 'which opened last spring'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The new library' - not the architect or city hall - is what opened last spring; the comma confirms this is extra, non-defining detail about a specific, already-identified library.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward from 'which' - what actually 'opened last spring'?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The witness ___ testimony contradicted the officer's report was cross-examined for hours.
quests.completedSentence: The witness whose testimony contradicted the officer's report was cross-examined for hours.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is correct because the testimony belongs to the witness - a possessive link, not a direct action.
quests.nativeTip: Check what belongs to the witness, rather than what the witness is doing directly.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The contractor ___ we hired last spring finally finished the renovation.
quests.completedSentence: The contractor (no word needed) we hired last spring finally finished the renovation.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' is the subject of 'hired,' making 'the contractor' the object; since there are no commas here, this defining clause allows the pronoun to be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'we' already has a job in this clause, and whether any commas are signaling extra information.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The findings of the three-year clinical trial that researchers just published have sparked global debate. What is the antecedent of 'that researchers just published'?
quests.completedSentence: The findings of the three-year clinical trial that researchers just published have sparked global debate. What is the antecedent of 'that researchers just published'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The findings' - not 'the trial' - is what was published; 'of the three-year clinical trial' is simply a prepositional phrase modifying 'findings.'
quests.nativeTip: 'Of the three-year clinical trial' just describes what kind of findings - check what was actually published.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The director of operations for the northeast region ___ handled the crisis received a company-wide commendation.
quests.completedSentence: The director of operations for the northeast region who handled the crisis received a company-wide commendation.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The director' - a person - is who handled the crisis, so 'who' is correct despite the long descriptive phrase in between.
quests.nativeTip: Strip away 'of operations for the northeast region' - it's all just describing which director. Who actually handled the crisis?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The headquarters of the multinational corporation, which relocated to Singapore last year, now employs over ten thousand people. What is the antecedent of 'which relocated to Singapore last year'?
quests.completedSentence: The headquarters of the multinational corporation, which relocated to Singapore last year, now employs over ten thousand people. What is the antecedent of 'which relocated to Singapore last year'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The headquarters' - not 'the corporation' itself - is what relocated; the comma confirms this is non-defining extra detail about a specific, already-identified headquarters.
quests.nativeTip: 'Of the multinational corporation' just tells you whose headquarters - check what actually relocated.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.targetClause: The Amazon Rainforest, which produces roughly 20% of the world's oxygen, spans several countries.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence uses punctuation correctly?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the Amazon Rainforest is a unique, one-of-a-kind place, the fact about oxygen production is non-defining extra information, requiring commas and 'which' rather than 'that.'
quests.nativeTip: Think about whether there could be more than one 'Amazon Rainforest' - does this detail need to narrow anything down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The Amazon Rainforest, which produces roughly 20% of the world's oxygen, spans several countries."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which of the following is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetClause: Employees who arrive after 9 a.m. must sign in at the front desk.
quests.completedSentence: Which of the following is correctly punctuated?
quests.ruleExplanation: This rule logically applies only to employees who arrive late, not all employees, so the clause is defining and needs no commas.
quests.nativeTip: Think about whether this rule is meant to apply to all employees or just some of them.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Employees who arrive after 9 a.m. must sign in at the front desk."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: My phone, ___ I've had for five years, finally stopped working.
quests.completedSentence: My phone, which I've had for five years, finally stopped working.
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas signal a non-defining clause, since 'my phone' is already unique - which rules out both 'that' and omission, leaving 'which' as the only correct choice.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas already surrounding this clause - what does that tell you about whether 'that' or omission would work here?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: The board of directors received a formal memo stating: 'The candidate whom the committee unanimously recommended will assume the role of Chief Financial Officer.' Is 'whom' used correctly here?
quests.targetClause: Yes, because the candidate is the object of 'recommended,' and formal writing favors 'whom'
quests.completedSentence: The board of directors received a formal memo stating: 'The candidate whom the committee unanimously recommended will assume the role of Chief Financial Officer.' Is 'whom' used correctly here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The committee' is the subject of 'recommended,' making 'the candidate' the object; 'whom' correctly marks this role and fits the formal register of the memo.
quests.nativeTip: Check who is doing the recommending, and who is being recommended - then consider the setting this sentence appears in.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Yes, because the candidate is the object of 'recommended,' and formal writing favors 'whom'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: A text message reads: 'omg the guy I met at your party last night just texted me!!' Is the omission of the relative pronoun before 'I met' acceptable here?
quests.targetClause: Yes, because casual speech and writing naturally drop object relative pronouns
quests.completedSentence: A text message reads: 'omg the guy I met at your party last night just texted me!!' Is the omission of the relative pronoun before 'I met' acceptable here?
quests.ruleExplanation: Casual speech and writing, like text messages, naturally drop object relative pronouns; this omission is completely standard and expected here.
quests.nativeTip: Think about the setting this message was written in, and how people naturally speak or text in that kind of context.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Yes, because casual speech and writing naturally drop object relative pronouns"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which version fits the formal tone of a legal deposition transcript, given there is only one defendant in this case?
quests.targetClause: The defendant, whom investigators questioned for six hours, ultimately confessed.
quests.completedSentence: Which version fits the formal tone of a legal deposition transcript, given there is only one defendant in this case?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' matches the formal legal register, and since there's only one defendant, commas are required on both sides of this non-defining clause.
quests.nativeTip: Since there's only one defendant in this case, check for both correct comma placement and the more formal object pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The defendant, whom investigators questioned for six hours, ultimately confessed."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The novelist who wrote three bestsellers, whose latest book was just adapted into a film, will speak at the festival. Which clause is defining, and which is non-defining?
quests.targetClause: 'who wrote three bestsellers' is defining; 'whose latest book was just adapted into a film' is non-defining.
quests.completedSentence: The novelist who wrote three bestsellers, whose latest book was just adapted into a film, will speak at the festival. Which clause is defining, and which is non-defining?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who wrote three bestsellers' has no commas and helps identify which novelist - defining. 'Whose latest book was just adapted into a film,' set off by a comma, adds extra detail about this specific novelist - non-defining.
quests.nativeTip: Check the punctuation around each clause separately.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'who wrote three bestsellers' is defining; 'whose latest book was just adapted into a film' is non-defining."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correctly constructed, given that there are several nominees but only one award ceremony this year?
quests.targetClause: The nominee who won the award, which took place downtown, gave an emotional speech.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correctly constructed, given that there are several nominees but only one award ceremony this year?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who won the award' is defining, since there are multiple nominees; 'which took place downtown' is non-defining, since there's only one award ceremony this year.
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause against its own antecedent separately - 'nominee' has several candidates, 'award ceremony' has only one this year.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The nominee who won the award, which took place downtown, gave an emotional speech."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The email from the client, which arrived just before the deadline, mentioned a change that would affect the entire timeline. What does 'that would affect the entire timeline' describe?
quests.completedSentence: The email from the client, which arrived just before the deadline, mentioned a change that would affect the entire timeline. What does 'that would affect the entire timeline' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'A change' - the specific change mentioned in the email - is what would affect the timeline, making this a separate defining clause from the non-defining one describing the email's arrival.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward from 'that' - what would actually 'affect the entire timeline'?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The letter from the lawyer at the downtown office that finally arrived settled the entire dispute. What is the antecedent of 'that finally arrived'?
quests.completedSentence: The letter from the lawyer at the downtown office that finally arrived settled the entire dispute. What is the antecedent of 'that finally arrived'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The letter' - not the lawyer or the office - is what arrived; both 'from the lawyer' and 'at the downtown office' are just descriptive phrases.
quests.nativeTip: Two decoys stand between the true antecedent and 'that' - a person and a place. What actually 'arrived'?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The invitation from my cousin in Chicago, which I almost missed in my spam folder, arrived just in time. What is the antecedent of 'which I almost missed in my spam folder'?
quests.completedSentence: The invitation from my cousin in Chicago, which I almost missed in my spam folder, arrived just in time. What is the antecedent of 'which I almost missed in my spam folder'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The invitation' - not the cousin or Chicago - is what was almost missed; the comma confirms this is non-defining detail about a specific, already-identified invitation.
quests.nativeTip: Two decoys - a person and a place - sit between the true antecedent and 'which.' What did 'I' actually almost miss?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The proposal from the marketing team for the spring campaign ___ ultimately won approval from the board.
quests.completedSentence: The proposal from the marketing team for the spring campaign which ultimately won approval from the board.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The proposal' - a thing - is what won approval, so 'which' is correct despite two descriptive phrases sitting in between.
quests.nativeTip: Strip away 'from the marketing team' and 'for the spring campaign' - both are just descriptive detail. What actually won approval?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The venue ___ we finally booked for the wedding has a stunning garden.
quests.completedSentence: The venue (no word needed) we finally booked for the wedding has a stunning garden.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We' is the subject of 'booked,' making 'the venue' the object; since this is a defining clause about a thing, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'We' already has a job in this clause - 'booked.' Does this defining clause allow the pronoun to disappear?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Relative Adverb (when)
quests.questionSentence: The morning ___ we exchanged vows is one I'll never forget.
quests.completedSentence: The morning (no word needed) we exchanged vows is one I'll never forget.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'When' can be omitted here, just as in earlier lessons - 'the morning we exchanged vows' is a natural, complete way to express this defining time clause.
quests.nativeTip: This relative adverb of time can often be dropped in natural, everyday English, just like object pronouns can.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Our wedding day, ___ we'll always remember fondly, was absolutely perfect.
quests.completedSentence: Our wedding day, which we'll always remember fondly, was absolutely perfect.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because this is a non-defining clause, signaled by the commas since 'our wedding day' is already unique, the pronoun cannot be omitted, and 'that' is banned after a comma - 'which' is the only correct choice.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas here - does that change whether this pronoun, even though it's an object relative, could ever be dropped?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The defendant's attorney, who has practiced law for over two decades, requested a continuance. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.targetClause: Non-defining - 'the defendant's attorney' already refers to one specific person, so the experience detail is extra.
quests.completedSentence: The defendant's attorney, who has practiced law for over two decades, requested a continuance. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The defendant's attorney' already identifies one specific person, so the experience detail is non-defining extra information, correctly set off with commas.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how many attorneys 'the defendant's attorney' could refer to - one specific one, or several needing narrowing down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Non-defining - 'the defendant's attorney' already refers to one specific person, so the experience detail is extra."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The medication that the specialist initially prescribed, which caused an unexpected allergic reaction, was immediately discontinued. What does 'which caused an unexpected allergic reaction' describe?
quests.completedSentence: The medication that the specialist initially prescribed, which caused an unexpected allergic reaction, was immediately discontinued. What does 'which caused an unexpected allergic reaction' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The medication' - not the specialist - is what caused the reaction; this is a second, non-defining clause adding extra detail about the medication already identified by the first, defining clause.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward from 'which' - what actually caused the reaction?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The hypothesis ___ the research team spent years testing was ultimately disproven by newer data.
quests.completedSentence: The hypothesis (no word needed) the research team spent years testing was ultimately disproven by newer data.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The research team' is the subject of 'spent... testing,' making 'the hypothesis' the object; since it's a thing in a defining clause, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'The research team' already has a job in this clause. Does this defining clause about a thing allow the pronoun to disappear?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: Local officials confirmed that the bridge, which has been closed for repairs since March, will reopen next month. What does 'which has been closed for repairs since March' describe?
quests.completedSentence: Local officials confirmed that the bridge, which has been closed for repairs since March, will reopen next month. What does 'which has been closed for repairs since March' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The bridge' - not local officials or next month - is what has been closed for repairs; the comma confirms this is non-defining detail about a specific, already-identified bridge.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward from 'which' - what has actually been closed?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The report ___ the agency released Tuesday revealed significant funding gaps.
quests.completedSentence: The report (no word needed) the agency released Tuesday revealed significant funding gaps.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The agency' is the subject of 'released,' making 'the report' the object; since it's a thing in a defining clause, the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'The agency' already has a job in this clause. Does this defining clause about a thing allow the pronoun to disappear?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The senator, whom several colleagues have publicly criticized, defended the controversial vote. Why is 'whom' (not 'who') used here?
quests.targetClause: Because 'the senator' is the object of 'criticized' - 'colleagues' is the subject.
quests.completedSentence: The senator, whom several colleagues have publicly criticized, defended the controversial vote. Why is 'whom' (not 'who') used here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Colleagues' is the subject of 'have criticized,' making 'the senator' the object - which calls for 'whom,' regardless of the news context.
quests.nativeTip: Check who is doing the criticizing, and who is being criticized.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Because 'the senator' is the object of 'criticized' - 'colleagues' is the subject."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The keys to the safe deposit box that my grandmother left me were nowhere to be found. What is the antecedent of 'that my grandmother left me'?
quests.completedSentence: The keys to the safe deposit box that my grandmother left me were nowhere to be found. What is the antecedent of 'that my grandmother left me'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The keys' - not the safe deposit box itself - is what my grandmother left me; 'to the safe deposit box' is simply a prepositional phrase describing which keys.
quests.nativeTip: 'To the safe deposit box' just tells you what the keys open - check what my grandmother actually left me.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The inheritance, ___ my grandmother carefully organized before she passed, included several family heirlooms.
quests.completedSentence: The inheritance, which my grandmother carefully organized before she passed, included several family heirlooms.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because this is a non-defining clause, signaled by the commas, the pronoun cannot be omitted and 'that' cannot be used; 'which' is the only correct choice.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas - does that change whether this pronoun could ever be dropped, or whether 'that' could be used?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The heirloom that meant the most to her, a silver locket which had belonged to her own mother, was passed down to me. Which of the following is true about the two relative clauses in this sentence?
quests.targetClause: 'that meant the most to her' is a defining relative clause; 'which had belonged to her own mother' is a non-defining relative clause describing 'a silver locket.'
quests.completedSentence: The heirloom that meant the most to her, a silver locket which had belonged to her own mother, was passed down to me. Which of the following is true about the two relative clauses in this sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That meant the most to her' has no commas and identifies which heirloom - defining. 'Which had belonged to her own mother,' set off by commas, adds extra detail about 'a silver locket' - non-defining.
quests.nativeTip: Check the punctuation around each clause separately, and what noun each one attaches to.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'that meant the most to her' is a defining relative clause; 'which had belonged to her own mother' is a non-defining relative clause describing 'a silver locket.'"
